name: Challenger
intro: This is the bottom half of Challenger, the last Apollo lander, which brought Gene Cernan and geologist Harrison Schmitt to the Taurus-Littrow valley on 11 December 1972. They explored for three days. When they left, it stayed behind as their launch pad, and no one has walked on the Moon since.

hotspots.title: The last plaque
hotspots.text: The plaque on the ladder reads: “Here man completed his first explorations of the Moon, December 1972 A.D. May the spirit of peace in which we came be reflected in the lives of all mankind.”

photo.alt: An astronaut’s arm and a ladder on the side of the lunar module, with a small metal plaque fixed to the ladder.
photo.caption: Gene Cernan at the ladder, with the plaque that stayed behind.

hotspots.title: The last footprints
hotspots.text: Gene Cernan climbed this ladder last. His bootprints at the bottom are the most recent human footprints on the Moon.

source.label: Apollo Lunar Surface Journal: Apollo 17 EVA-3 close-out

hotspots.title: Orange soil
hotspots.text: On the second moonwalk, Schmitt found a patch of orange soil. It turned out to be made of tiny glass beads from volcanic fire fountains billions of years ago.

hotspots.title: The landing engine
hotspots.text: This engine set Challenger down in a narrow valley between tall mountains.

hotspots.title: The missing top half
hotspots.text: The cabin blasted off from here on 14 December 1972, and the rover’s TV camera followed it into the black sky.

source.label: Apollo Lunar Surface Journal: Apollo 17 return to orbit

funFact: Before climbing aboard for the last time, Gene Cernan said: “We leave as we came and, God willing, as we shall return, with peace and hope for all mankind.”
whyLeft: Nothing broke: the bottom half was built to stay behind as a launch pad for the cabin.
repurpose: Its tanks are empty, but it marks the last human visit to the Moon. Future explorers could photograph it as a 50-year record of how hardware ages here.
